title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 184
paragraphs: Up to this point, and as far as Thermopylae, the army had suffered no disaster; and by my reckoning its numbers were still as follows. Of the 1,207 ships that had come from Asia, the original crews supplied by the various nations amounted to 241,400 men — reckoning 200 men per ship. On each of these ships, in addition to the native fighting men, there served thirty Persian, Median, or Sacan marines, amounting to 36,210 more. To this and the previous numbers I will add the crews of the fifty-oared galleys, estimating eighty men, more or less, in each. Of these vessels, as was mentioned earlier, there were 3,000 gathered together, which would yield 240,000 men. This, then, was the naval force from Asia, totaling 517,610 in all. The infantry numbered 1,700,000, and the cavalry 80,000; and to these I will add the Arabian camel-drivers and the Libyan charioteers, reckoning them at 20,000. The result is that the combined naval and land forces amount to 2,317,610 men. This is the tally of the army brought up out of Asia itself, not counting the attendants who accompanied it or the grain-transports and the men who sailed in them.
